sections.b: At the height of his reign God appears to Solomon a second time and sets the conditions plainly: obedience keeps David's throne, other gods will cost Israel the land and the temple (1 Kings 9:1–9). The chapters that follow show the height, the queen of Sheba's visit, 666 talents of gold a year, a lion throne and fourteen hundred chariots (1 Kings 10), and then the fall: seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines who turn his heart to Ashtoreth, Milcom and Chemosh in his old age (1 Kings 11:1–8). God raises opponents, and the prophet Ahijah tears a cloak to show the kingdom torn from his son (1 Kings 11:9–40). Readers have long noticed that gold, horses from Egypt and many wives are exactly what Deuteronomy's law of the king forbids (Deuteronomy 17:16–17).

common: Solomon's wealth and his many foreign wives led him away from the LORD in his old age, and the kingdom split after his death as a result.
uncommon: A rabbinic view holds that Solomon never worshiped idols himself but failed to stop his wives, and Scripture counts it against him as if he had (Shabbat 56b).

sections.b: The queen hears of Solomon's fame "tied to the name of the LORD" and comes to test him with riddles (chidot), bringing camels loaded with spices, gold and precious stones (1 Kings 10:1–2). Solomon answers everything; she sees his house, his table, his servants and his worship, and it leaves her breathless (1 Kings 10:3–5). Her speech is the chapter's center: the report was true, the half was not told, and the LORD made Solomon king "to do what is just and right" (1 Kings 10:6–9). The two exchange royal gifts, and she goes home (1 Kings 10:10–13). The narrator says nothing about romance or a child; those belong to later Ethiopian, Jewish and Islamic traditions.

common: The queen of Sheba came from southern Arabia (Yemen) or, in Ethiopian tradition, from Ethiopia.
uncommon: Some historians think the visit was told back into Solomon's reign from later contacts with Arabian queens known from 8th-century Assyrian records.

claude.title: Claude's note: a foreigner who names the purpose of kingship
claude.body: In 1 Kings 10 the clearest statement of what a king of Israel is for comes not from a prophet or priest but from a foreign queen: the LORD made him king "to do what is just and right" (1 Kings 10:9). My suggestion is that the narrator places this line deliberately, just before the inventory of gold, horses and wives that will bring Solomon down, so that a Gentile voice sets the standard by which Israel's king is about to fail.

sections.b: After the dedication, God promises that his eyes and heart will be on the house Solomon built, but warns that if Israel turns to other gods he will throw the house out of his sight and passersby will whistle at its ruin (1 Kings 9:3–9). Within five years of Solomon's death Shishak of Egypt empties its treasury (1 Kings 14:25–26), and Asa strips it again to pay Aram (1 Kings 15:18). Jeroboam's rival shrines at Bethel and Dan are built to keep the north from going up to it (1 Kings 12:26–29).

After twenty years of building, Solomon pays Hiram with twenty towns in Galilee, which Hiram calls the land of Cabul, "like nothing" (1 Kings 9:10–13). Hiram's sailors then crew Solomon's Red Sea fleet to Ophir (1 Kings 9:26–28; 1 Kings 10:11, 22). Chronicles tells the town exchange the other way round (2 Chronicles 8:1–2).

1 Kings 9:15 lists Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer among the cities Solomon built with forced labor. Yigael Yadin matched the verse with six-chambered gates at all three sites and dated them to Solomon; Israel Finkelstein and others have redated them to the 9th century, while Amihai Mazar, William Dever and others defend a 10th-century date for at least some. The verse is the center of the debate over how large Solomon's kingdom really was. The trade in chapter 10 (gold of Ophir, horses from Que, Tarshish ships) raises the same question.

The queen of Sheba tests Solomon's wisdom with riddles and finds it greater than the report (1 Kings 10:1–7), and "all the earth" seeks to hear the wisdom God put in his heart (1 Kings 10:24). The same chapter and the next show that wisdom does not guarantee faithfulness: the wisest king is turned by his wives (1 Kings 11:4). His son Rehoboam is offered wise counsel by the elders and rejects it (1 Kings 12:6–14).

sections.h: The king's law broken and the servant-king refused
sections.b: Solomon's later years read like a checklist against Deuteronomy's law of the king: gold and silver piled up, horses from Egypt, many wives who turn his heart (1 Kings 10:14–29; 1 Kings 11:1–4; Deuteronomy 17:16–17). Samuel's warning about the king's yoke comes true in forced labor (1 Samuel 8:11–17; 1 Kings 9:15; 1 Kings 12:4). At Shechem the elders offer Rehoboam a different model, a king who serves his people (1 Kings 12:7), and he refuses it. The queen of Sheba names the king's true task: "to do what is just and right" (1 Kings 10:9).
sections.refs: 1 Kings 10:9; 1 Kings 10:14–29; 1 Kings 11:1–4; 1 Kings 12:1–16; Deuteronomy 17:14–20; 1 Samuel 8:11–18

sections.b: The gold that came to Solomon each year weighed six hundred and sixty-six talents (1 Kings 10:14; 2 Chronicles 9:13). Some interpreters think Revelation's number of the beast (Revelation 13:18) deliberately recalls this figure, a king corrupted by wealth; most read Revelation's 666 as the numerical value of a name. The connection is possible, not proven.

Solomon had seven hundred wives of royal rank and three hundred concubines, many of them foreign princesses from treaty partners (1 Kings 11:1–3). Kings does not condemn the number as such but the result: "his wives bent his heart away" to other gods (1 Kings 11:3–4), as Deuteronomy warned (Deuteronomy 17:17). The Talmud uses Solomon to explain why the Torah usually does not give reasons for its laws: he thought he could keep the reason without the rule (Sanhedrin 21b).

sections.h: From Solomon's shrines to Jeroboam's calves
sections.b: These chapters move from Solomon's high places for Ashtoreth, Chemosh and Milcom (1 Kings 11:5–8) to Jeroboam's calves at Bethel and Dan (1 Kings 12:28–30), to Judah's standing stones and Asherah poles (1 Kings 14:23), Asa's purge of the "filthy idols" (gillulim, 1 Kings 15:12), and Ahab's temple of Baal in Samaria (1 Kings 16:31–33). Kings counts the calves, although they claimed to represent the God of the exodus, as "other gods" (1 Kings 14:9), and calls idols "puffs of air" (hevel, 1 Kings 16:13).

Solomon follows Ashtoreth (Astarte), goddess of the Sidonians (1 Kings 11:5). Asherah poles spread in both kingdoms (1 Kings 14:15, 23); Asa removes his mother as queen mother for making a "horrid thing" for Asherah (1 Kings 15:13). Ahab marries Jezebel of Tyre, serves Baal, builds him a temple in Samaria and sets up an Asherah pole (1 Kings 16:31–33), the background to Elijah's contest on Carmel (1 Kings 18).
sections.refs: 1 Kings 11:5; 1 Kings 11:33; 1 Kings 14:15; 1 Kings 14:23; 1 Kings 15:13; 1 Kings 16:31–33

sections.b: 1 Kings 11:7 says Solomon built a high place for "Molech, the vile idol of the Ammonites," while 11:5 and 11:33 name the Ammonite god Milcom. Many scholars think Milcom is meant and the two names, both from the root for "king," were confused. Nothing in Kings suggests Solomon offered children.

In 1 Kings 11 the word satan means a human enemy. Solomon had boasted of rest with "no satan" (1 Kings 5:4); now the LORD raises up Hadad of Edom and Rezon of Damascus as satans against him (1 Kings 11:14, 23, 25). The usage shows how the word worked before it became the name of a spiritual adversary.

A boy of Edom's royal family escapes Joab's slaughter, grows up at Pharaoh's court, marries the queen's sister, and returns after David's and Joab's deaths to trouble Solomon (1 Kings 11:14–22). The Greek text has him rule in Edom (1 Kings 11:25). Edom's independence grew in the following century (2 Kings 8:20–22).

Ahijah's torn cloak gives Jeroboam ten tribes and the offer of "a house that lasts" like David's, if he keeps God's commands (1 Kings 11:29–38). Instead he builds a religion to protect his throne: calves at Bethel and Dan, new priests, a new feast date (1 Kings 12:26–33). He ignores the sign of the split altar and his own healed hand (1 Kings 13:1–6, 33). When his son falls sick, Ahijah sentences his house (1 Kings 14:1–16), and Baasha carries it out (1 Kings 15:29). The long Greek supplement at 12:24 tells his story a second time with other details.

common: Jeroboam's calves were idols, and his sin set the northern kingdom on the road to destruction.
uncommon: Many historians think Jeroboam's bulls were pedestals for the invisible LORD, like the cherubim in Jerusalem, and that Bethel and Dan were old shrines of Israel's God.

sections.b: Kings gives three causes side by side. God's judgment: the LORD tears the kingdom from Solomon's son because of Solomon's idolatry (1 Kings 11:11–13, 31–33), and the split is "a turn" from the LORD (1 Kings 12:15, 24). A king's folly: Rehoboam rejects the elders' advice to serve the people and threatens scorpions instead (1 Kings 12:6–14). Tribal politics: the north meets at its own center, Shechem, raises Sheba's old cry against David's house, and stones the labor chief (1 Kings 12:1, 16–18; 2 Samuel 20:1). Historians stress the third; the narrator holds all three together. Afterward the two kingdoms fight along the Benjamin border (1 Kings 14:30; 1 Kings 15:16–22) and their histories run side by side.

Rehoboam goes to Shechem to be made king by the northern tribes, and there they reject him (1 Kings 12:1–16). Jeroboam then fortifies Shechem as his first capital (1 Kings 12:25); he also fortified Penuel, and later the court is at Tirzah (1 Kings 14:17).

Jeroboam makes two calves of gold and presents them with Aaron's words: "Here are your gods, Israel, that brought you up from the land of Egypt!" (1 Kings 12:28; compare Exodus 32:4). He sets one at Bethel and one at Dan (1 Kings 12:29). Ahijah calls them "other gods, images of cast metal" (1 Kings 14:9), the same word used for Aaron's calf. When the man of God's sign strikes Jeroboam's hand, the king asks him to "beg the LORD your God to soften" (1 Kings 13:6), the words used of Moses pleading after the first calf (Exodus 32:11). Scholars debate whether the calves were meant as idols or as pedestals for the invisible God; Hosea mocked them either way (Hosea 8:5–6; Hosea 13:2).
sections.refs: 1 Kings 12:26–33; 1 Kings 13:6; 1 Kings 14:9; Exodus 32:4; Exodus 32:11; Hosea 8:5–6; Hosea 10:5; Hosea 13:2; 2 Kings 10:29

sections.b: Jeroboam sets a gold calf at Bethel, stations priests there and goes up on its altar at his new autumn feast (1 Kings 12:29–33). A man of God from Judah condemns the altar and names Josiah as the king who will defile it; the altar splits (1 Kings 13:1–5). An old prophet of Bethel deceives the man of God and then buries him (1 Kings 13:11–32). The prophecy is fulfilled in 2 Kings 23:15–18.

Jeroboam put his second calf at Dan, the northern shrine whose priesthood traced its line to Moses (1 Kings 12:29–30; Judges 18:30). The people went in procession "all the way to Dan" (1 Kings 12:30). At Tel Dan, Avraham Biran excavated a large cult platform and a horned altar that he linked with Jeroboam's sanctuary. Ben-hadad of Damascus struck Dan in Asa's time (1 Kings 15:20).

Solomon builds high places for Chemosh and Molech on the mountain facing Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:7), which last until Josiah (2 Kings 23:13). Jeroboam makes "a house of high places" with his own priests (1 Kings 12:31; 1 Kings 13:33). Judah builds them "on every high hill and under every leafy tree" (1 Kings 14:23). Asa is a good king, but "the high places were not taken away" (1 Kings 15:14).
sections.refs: 1 Kings 11:7; 1 Kings 12:31–32; 1 Kings 13:2; 1 Kings 13:32–33; 1 Kings 14:23; 1 Kings 15:14

sections.h: Prophets who make and unmake kings
sections.b: In 1 Kings 11–16 prophets shape the history. Ahijah of Shiloh tears his cloak to give Jeroboam ten tribes (1 Kings 11:29–39) and later announces the end of his house (1 Kings 14:7–16). Shemaiah stops a civil war (1 Kings 12:22–24). A man of God from Judah condemns the altar at Bethel and is himself deceived by another prophet (1 Kings 13). Jehu son of Hanani sentences Baasha (1 Kings 16:1–4, 7). Each word is shown coming true (1 Kings 15:29; 1 Kings 16:12, 34), a pattern Gerhard von Rad saw as the backbone of the history in Kings.

sections.h: Why the man of God died
sections.b: Readers have long been troubled that the deceived prophet dies while the liar lives. Common answers: he had heard God's command directly and should not have set it aside for a secondhand claim (Deuteronomy 13:1–3); his death made the word against Bethel all the more certain; the story is meant to show how seriously God's word must be taken. The narrator does not soften it, but he gives the man of God an honored grave that Josiah later spares (1 Kings 13:30–32; 2 Kings 23:17–18).

common: The man of God was punished because he disobeyed a direct command from God, even though he was deceived.
uncommon: Karl Barth read the two prophets as Judah and Israel, the elect and the rejected, who need each other and lie in one grave.

sections.b: Shishak shelters Jeroboam (1 Kings 11:40) and in Rehoboam's fifth year comes up against Jerusalem and takes the treasures of the temple and palace, including Solomon's gold shields (1 Kings 14:25–26). Rehoboam replaces them with bronze (1 Kings 14:27–28). His Karnak list names many towns of the northern kingdom too, including Penuel, which Jeroboam had fortified (1 Kings 12:25).

sections.h: Where the numbers in 1 Kings 14–16 strain
sections.b: Several puzzles appear in these chapters. Omri's twelve years (1 Kings 16:23) overlap the civil war with Tibni (1 Kings 16:15, 21–22). Chronicles dates Baasha's attack on Asa to Asa's thirty-sixth year (2 Chronicles 16:1), although by Kings Baasha died in Asa's twenty-sixth (1 Kings 16:8). Rehoboam is forty-one at his accession in the Hebrew but sixteen in the Greek supplement (1 Kings 14:21; 1 Kings 12:24). The Greek also dates Jehoshaphat differently (1 Kings 16:28). Thiele's system explains many of these by overlap and counting methods; others see different sources.
sections.refs: 1 Kings 14:20–21; 1 Kings 15:1–2; 1 Kings 15:9–10; 1 Kings 15:33; 1 Kings 16:8; 1 Kings 16:15–23; 1 Kings 16:29; 2 Chronicles 16:1

sections.b: Solomon took Ammonite wives and built a high place for the Ammonite god, called Milcom and Molech (1 Kings 11:1, 5, 7, 33). One of those wives, Naamah the Ammonite, was the mother of Rehoboam and so of every later king of Judah (1 Kings 14:21, 31). The Talmud names her with Ruth the Moabite as the "two good doves" for whose sake Ammon and Moab were spared (Bava Kamma 38b).

Omri, the army commander, is proclaimed king in the camp at Gibbethon, besieges Tirzah, outlasts Tibni and reigns twelve years (1 Kings 16:15–23). He buys the hill of Samaria and builds his capital (1 Kings 16:24). The verdict is that he "did worse than all who were before him" (1 Kings 16:25), and his achievements are left to the lost records (1 Kings 16:27). Outside sources fill the gap.

Omri bought the hill from Shemer for two talents of silver and named his city after him (1 Kings 16:24). Ahab built a temple of Baal there (1 Kings 16:32). An earlier verse already speaks of "the towns of Samaria" in Jeroboam's time, using the name of the narrator's day (1 Kings 13:32).

Ahab marries Jezebel, daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians, and then serves Baal and builds him a temple in Samaria (1 Kings 16:31–32). Josephus, quoting the Tyrian historian Menander, names her father Ittobaal, a priest of Astarte who seized the throne of Tyre (Against Apion 1.123). The marriage sealed an alliance between Israel and Phoenicia, as Solomon's foreign marriages had.

In Ahab's days Hiel of Bethel rebuilt Jericho, laying its foundation "with Abiram his firstborn" and setting up its gates "with Segub his youngest," fulfilling Joshua's curse (1 Kings 16:34; Joshua 6:26). Readers debate whether the sons died under the curse or were offered as foundation sacrifices.

From 1 Kings 14 on, the history is laid out in regnal frames: a synchronism, the length of reign, a verdict measured by David or by Jeroboam, a few events, a citation of the lost royal records, and the burial (1 Kings 14:19–31; 1 Kings 15:1–34; 1 Kings 16:1–34). Prophetic words are announced and then shown fulfilled (1 Kings 14:10–11 with 1 Kings 15:29; 1 Kings 16:1–4 with 1 Kings 16:12). The note that Israel had rebelled "to this day" (1 Kings 12:19) suggests older sources written before 722 BC.

God's second word to Solomon ties the throne to obedience (1 Kings 9:4–7), yet when Solomon fails God keeps one tribe "for the sake of David" so that David may have "a lamp" in Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:13, 36; 1 Kings 15:4). He humbles David's line, "though not for all time" (1 Kings 11:39). Jeroboam is offered "a house that lasts" on the same terms (1 Kings 11:38).

sections.h: Jeroboam's feast in the eighth month
sections.b: Jeroboam held a feast "like the festival held in Judah" on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, a month later than the Feast of Booths in Leviticus 23:34 (1 Kings 12:32–33). Kings says he devised it from his own heart; some scholars think the north kept an older or later harvest calendar.
